title: Veteran Spotlight: Bryan’s Path from the Army National Guard to Array Labs
summary: Array Labs is working to provide high-quality 3D imagery on a global scale.
body_markdown:
Bryan was driving to school on the morning of September 11, 2001, when the first plane hit. “It was one of those things you knew that the world instantly changed.” He watched the second one on TV after classes were shut down. “From then on, I was like, yeah, I’m gonna join.” His dad told him to finish college first.


He did, then life moved on. College friends left school to join the military. “I felt I didn’t deserve the freedoms I had,” he says. “I know that sounds kind of corny.”


On the 10th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, Bryan was working as an aerospace engineer. “You blink and you’re 29. I realized that if I didn’t do it, it just wasn’t going to happen.” He quit his job on September 11, 2011. By September 30, he was swearing in to the Army National Guard. At bootcamp his fellow recruits called him Grandpa.


He commissioned as a second lieutenant out of Fort Benning and served as an infantry officer for his entire career. His assignments included heavy weapons platoon leader, scout sniper platoon leader, and senior infantry instructor at Officer Candidate School.


The Guard also has a stateside mission. Bryan sums it up as floods, fires, and riots. He worked on fire crews, ran search and rescue, and was deployed for a number of natural disasters throughout the state. Why did he stay for 14 years? “Oh, the people. I still talk to everyone, to this day, all the time.”


Bryan’s civilian career moved from engineering to recruiting. He has spent 12 years in talent acquisition, sourcing and hiring for cleared technical roles across aerospace and defense. He made the jump after finding he enjoyed helping people find meaningful careers.


Veterans are a natural fit for that work, he says. They stay flexible and support the mission while still thinking critically about it. “The enthusiasm and the will and the commitment was typically higher than their peers. They want to be here.”


He sees the same values at Array. “They take care of their people, and they deliver on the mission, and they do what it takes to get it done.” The Marines have a saying that he feels is especially fitting for work at a startup: Semper Gumby. Always flexible.


The habit carries into recruiting, where offers sometimes fall through after months of work, or evolving technologies can sometimes lead to strange encounters like candidates showing up to virtual interviews with an AI face filter on (an experience he described as “unnerving” and “very obviously fake”). “Change is a constant,” he says. His answer is to dust off and keep moving. “Just always, always forward.”


For Bryan, Veterans Day is a heavy holiday. At its core, he says, it honors the sacrifice of everyone who has served, not only in the United States but around the world. Some of that sacrifice is close to home. Several of Bryan’s friends from the Guard are no longer here.


Veterans Day is also an opportunity to recognize everyone who served. In Bryan’s words, “You get to just thank people for what they did.”


Thank you, Bryan, and thank you to every veteran across our workforce, our partners and our communities.
